prize_parts.citation: for the development of palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B052 as a single part for Hartwig and Buchwald. After reading all eight round-1 files, the case still rests on the chemistry. Buchwald and Hartwig independently built general, ligand-controlled palladium catalysts for aryl amination in the mid-1990s, then drove them through several ligand generations with real mechanistic work on oxidative addition, amine binding and reductive elimination. That turned a harsh, narrow reaction into a routine operation used in pharmaceutical process chemistry, agrochemicals and organic electronic materials, and it is visible in a very large number of later syntheses. Three decades of independent confirmation settle maturity, and the two-person attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist. The round-1 files did not weaken this. They moved the question to the Kosugi citation wording and to whether a second part is needed, and on both I think a narrow, single-part prize is the better answer.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains that the 2010 cross-coupling prize already honoured palladium catalysis, so this can be read as a sequel. I weigh it less than the critics because the new element was ligand design and mechanism for a heteroatom nucleophile, not a wider substrate table, and the 2010 laureates did not cover C-N bond formation. Kosugi's tin-amide coupling is a real precursor and a priority argument is possible, although I cannot settle it from the files. A citation worded for the catalytic amination of aryl halides with amines and a base does not depend on the precursor. Hartwig's presence on other candidates does not change the two-name attribution here. A purely synthetic-methods prize is also less dramatic than a biology-facing one, but that is not a criterion I will weight.

responses.point: Aili proposes a two-part prize pairing B052 (Buchwald, Hartwig) with B004 (Liu alone), arguing for balance between a mature synthetic method and a newer biomolecular tool, with the three-laureate limit split two plus one.
responses.response: I accept that the three-name cap makes the two-plus-one split feasible, but I do not think balance is a scientific reason to add a part. Base editing is real deaminase chemistry and the adenine editor, evolved from a deaminase with no DNA substrate, is new, which is why I keep it among my open items. But it sits close to the 2020 CRISPR prize, clinical durability and safety data are still arriving, and crediting Liu alone leaves out Komor and Gaudelli, whose first-author work you yourself call decisive. That is a weaker part than B052. Pairing a settled prize with a part that is contested on credit and maturity risks weakening the strongest case, and I would keep B052 alone.

responses.point: Aqvist supports B052 alone for Buchwald and Hartwig and lists the 2010 sequel objection and the Kosugi and Migita-type precursor question as his open concerns. He keeps B037 and B004 as alternatives.
responses.response: We are aligned on the configuration and on the two objections. On Migita, the 1980s tin and palladium work was mechanistically instructive but used stoichiometric toxic tin reagents and had narrow scope, so it is a precursor to the catalytic general method and not the method. On B037 we also agree that no approved degrader and a four-to-eight-name attribution fight are real obstacles. Where I am more cautious than you is B004: your Liu, Komor and Gaudelli attribution is cleaner than Aili's, but I would still rank it behind B037 as an alternative because of the closeness to CRISPR.

responses.point: Zou ranks B052 first as the only candidate with broad cross-subfield support and a clean two-laureate citation, and flags that his 1994 to 1995 timeline rests on recollection and that the Kosugi precedent needs wording.
responses.response: I agree with the conclusion and can help with the chronology you could not check. The independent Hartwig and Buchwald reports on catalytic amination appeared in 1995, and the case for general scope rests on the later ligand work, bulky biaryl phosphines for Buchwald and hindered alkylphosphines such as P(t-Bu)3 for Hartwig. The citation can lean on that generality, which would also answer your question about wording. I would not take your broader point about a second part pairing with a materials achievement. I am unconvinced B032 would be a better partner than a single part, since its attribution among Miyasaka, Park, Snaith, Kanatzidis and Seok is not resolved and stability and lead toxicity are open.

responses.point: Linke, the chair, ranks B002 first with Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen as a quantitative physical-chemical principle for membraneless compartmentalisation, and lists physiological relevance and the Chemistry versus Physiology or Medicine fit as open points. He lists B052 as his first alternative.
responses.response: I take the chair's own reservations seriously, since they match mine. The physiological relevance of liquid-like condensates is still disputed, and the decisive 2009 observation was imaging of P granules in cells, which is cell biology and soft-matter physics more than chemistry. The 2012 Rosen reconstitution is the stronger chemical foundation, but a citation built on it alone leaves out the in vivo discovery, and adding Pappu and Mittag breaks the three-name cap. You say attribution clarity and opening support of B052 might outweigh conceptual breadth. I would say it differently: the breadth of B002 is real, but a prize should rest on a result that has stopped being argued, and B052 has. I would not block B002 if the committee prefers it, which is why it stays among my alternatives.

responses.point: Chabes proposes B004 alone for Liu, Komor and Gaudelli as a biological process turned into well-defined chemistry, and puts B037 second. He concedes that Kondo and Nishida's Target-AID attribution and the 2020 CRISPR prize are open problems.
responses.response: I agree the mechanism is a clean chemical story and the directed evolution of the adenine deaminase is new chemistry. But your own caveats, Kondo and Nishida possibly displacing Komor or Gaudelli, prime editing sharing the Liu laboratory, and long-term safety data still emerging, are the reasons I rank it seventh and B052 first. Three decades of confirmation against a field still reporting its first clinical outcomes is the difference in maturity. I would watch B004 closely in later years, but I do not see it as ready this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat C-N coupling as too close to the 2010 cross-coupling prize, and I cannot resolve this from the files
Whether the citation should name Kosugi or be worded around the general catalytic amination with ligand control, leaving his tin-amide precursor outside
Whether other members will insist on a biology-facing second part, which I do not prefer on scientific grounds
Whether my chemistry-recollection of the 1995 publication dates and the ligand generations is exact, since I cannot check the literature in this exercise
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has appeared in round 1 or in the chair's summary. I have no collaboration with Buchwald or Hartwig. My link to the field is general, as a synthetic organic chemist who uses these methods, and I consider that insufficient for recusal. I also have no known tie to the other shortlisted laureates.
